title: Infections, hospital admissions and deaths involving COVID-19 continued to decrease in England
subtitle: Estimated COVID-19 positivity rates, hospital admissions and number of deaths, England, 1 August 2020 to 28 February 2021
commentary: Infections, hospital admissions and deaths involving COVID-19 all continued to decrease in England. The percentage of people testing positive for COVID-19 (positivity rate) fell to 0.45% in the week ending 27 February 2021. The hospital admission rate decreased to 8.4 per 100,000 people in the week ending 28 February. It is now four times lower than in mid-January. The number of registered deaths involving COVID-19 decreased by 28.8% to 2,772 in the week ending 26 February.
sourcename: null

title: The percentage of people testing positive continued to decrease in England, Wales, Northern Ireland and Scotland
subtitle: Official estimates of the percentage of the population in England, Wales, Northern Ireland and Scotland testing positive for the coronavirus (COVID-19) on nose and throat swabs, from 3 May 2020
commentary: The percentage of people testing positive for COVID-19 continued to decrease in all four UK nations in the week ending 27 February 2021. In England, it is estimated that 0.45% of the community population had COVID-19 (around 1 in 220 people). The estimated positivity rate was 0.35% in Wales (1 in 285 people), 0.31% in Northern Ireland (1 in 325 people) and 0.30% (1 in 335 people) in Scotland.
sourcename: Coronavirus (COVID-19) Infection Survey

title: The North East has the highest COVID-19 positivity rate
subtitle: Estimated percentage of the population testing positive for the coronavirus (COVID-19) on nose and throat swabs, by sub-regional geography, England, from modelling the most recent seven days of data, 21 to 27 February 2021
commentary: The highest positivity rate was seen in the North East of England, followed by the West Midlands in the week ending 27 February 2021. The South East and South West had the lowest percentages of people testing positive for COVID-19.
sourcename: Coronavirus (COVID-19) Infection Survey

title: Coronavirus (COVID-19) Infection Survey and Real-time Assessment of Community Transmission study show similar trends over time
subtitle: Estimated percentage of the community population testing positive for the coronavirus (COVID-19), 27 April 2020 to 27 February 2021, England
commentary:
The proportion of people testing positive for COVID-19 in England has decreased, according to both the Coronavirus (COVID-19) Infection Survey (CIS, 21 to 27 February 2021) and the Real-time Assessment of Community Transmission (REACT) study (6 to 23 February). REACT and CIS show similar trends over time. 
Both CIS and REACT reported lowest positivity rates in the oldest age groups: CIS among those aged 70 years and over and REACT among those aged 65 years and over.
CIS and REACT both estimate how many infections there are in the community, although they use different methods and publish data at different times.
sourcename: Real-time Assessment of Community Transmission (REACT) study

title: The percentage of people testing positive continued to decrease in most regions in England
subtitle: Estimated percentage of the population testing positive for the coronavirus (COVID-19) on nose and throat swabs, daily, by region, since 17 January 2021, England
commentary: The percentage of people testing positive has decreased in all regions in England in the most recent week (ending 27 February 2021), except for in the North East, East Midlands and East of England where the trend is uncertain. The North East has the highest positivity rate of all regions, while the South West has the lowest.
sourcename: Coronavirus (COVID-19) Infection Survey

title: The most commonly reported symptoms among people testing positive were cough, fatigue and headache
subtitle: Percentage of people with symptoms, including only those who have a strong positive test (cycle threshold (Ct) less than 30), from 1 October 2020 to 30 January 2021, UK countries
commentary: Cough, fatigue and headache were the most common symptoms reported in positive COVID-19 cases across the four UK countries. Abdominal pain, diarrhoea and nausea were less commonly reported. Similar trends in reported symptoms can be seen in all four UK countries.
sourcename: Coronavirus (COVID-19) Infection Survey: characteristics of people testing positive for COVID-19, countries of the UK

title: The percentage of people testing positive for COVID-19 has continued to decrease in most age groups
subtitle: Estimated percentage of the population testing positive for the coronavirus (COVID-19) on nose and throat swabs, daily, by age group, since 17 January 2021, England
commentary: The percentage of people testing positive for COVID-19 decreased in all age groups in the most recent week (ending 27 February 2021), except in secondary school-aged children (School Years 7 to 11) where the trends remain uncertain. Adults aged 25 to 34 years had the highest positivity rate (0.51%), while adults aged 70 years and over continued to have the lowest (0.23%).
sourcename: Coronavirus (COVID-19) Infection Survey

title: Individuals from the "Other than White" ethnic group had significantly greater positivity rates in the North West, Yorkshire and The Humber, East Midlands, West Midlands, and the South East
subtitle: The odds ratios of individuals in the "Other than White" ethnic group testing positive for coronavirus (COVID-19) on a swab test compared with individuals from the White ethnic group by region, England, between 4 October and 28 November 2020
commentary: Individuals from the "Other than White" ethnic group were more likely to test positive for the coronavirus (COVID-19) compared with those from the "White" ethnic group in the North West, Yorkshire and The Humber, East Midlands, West Midlands, and the South East. There was no evidence supporting a lower risk of testing positive in those from the "Other than White" ethnic group in any region. After adjusting for differential effects of ethnicity by region, there was no evidence that the effect of ethnicity varied over time or by age.
sourcename: Coronavirus (COVID-19) Infection Survey: characteristics of people testing positive for COVID-19 in England

title: Deaths involving COVID-19 decreased by 28.6% compared with the previous week
subtitle: Deaths involving and due to the coronavirus (COVID-19), and influenza and pneumonia, deaths registered in 2020 and 2021, England and Wales
commentary: In the week ending 26 February 2021, the number of deaths involving the coronavirus (COVID-19) registered in England and Wales decreased by 28.6% compared with the previous week, to 2,914. This accounted for nearly a quarter (23.1%) of all deaths registered that week. COVID-19 was the underlying cause of death for 84.7% of deaths listed as involving the disease. In contrast, only 10.6% of deaths involving influenza or pneumonia had these conditions listed as the underlying cause of death.
sourcename: Deaths registered weekly in England and Wales, provisional

title: The number of registered deaths was 9.2% above the five-year average in the latest week
subtitle: Number of deaths registered by week, England and Wales, 28 December 2019 to 26 February 2021
commentary: The total number of deaths registered between 13 March 2020 and 26 February 2021 in England and Wales was 628,736. Of these deaths, 132,090 mentioned the coronavirus (COVID-19) on the death certificate, equal to 21.0% of all deaths in England and Wales. In the latest week, deaths from all causes were 9.2% above the five-year average, but of those, the number of deaths not involving COVID-19 was below average.
sourcename: Deaths registered weekly in England and Wales, provisional

title: The number of deaths in the latest week was higher than the five-year average in most English regions and in Wales
subtitle: Number of deaths in Wales and regions in England, registered between 28 December 2019 and 26 February 2021
commentary: The number of deaths involving the coronavirus (COVID-19) decreased in all English regions in the latest week, with the largest decrease in the East of England. This is the fourth consecutive week where all English regions recorded a decrease. The total number of deaths registered was higher than the five-year average in most English regions, but below in the North East and South West. This is the first time since week ending 23 October 2020 that deaths in any English region have been below the five-year average. The area with the highest total deaths above the five-year average was the West Midlands, where total deaths were 19.7% higher than expected.
sourcename: Deaths registered weekly in England and Wales, provisional

title: Deaths due to COVID-19 by local area in England and Wales
subtitle: Number of deaths due to COVID-19 in Middle layer Super Output Areas, England and Wales, deaths registered between 1 March 2020 and 31 January 2021
commentary: The interactive map shows the cumulative number of monthly deaths due to COVID-19 in each area. Points on the map are placed at the centre of the local area they represent and do not show the actual location of deaths. The size of the circle is proportional to the number of deaths. Deaths “due to COVID-19” include only deaths where COVID-19 was the underlying cause of death.
sourcename: Monthly mortality analysis, England and Wales

title: The majority of deaths involving COVID-19 were in people aged 75 years and over in the latest week
subtitle: Number of deaths registered by week and age group, 28 December 2019 to 26 February 2021, England and Wales
commentary: Throughout the pandemic, most deaths have been seen in older age groups. In the week ending 26 February 2021, the majority (66.3%) of deaths involving the coronavirus (COVID-19) in England and Wales were in people aged 75 years and over. The number of deaths involving COVID-19 decreased or remained the same in all age groups (except those aged 10 to 14 years and 25 to 29 years, which increased by one and four deaths respectively). The biggest decrease was seen in those aged 90 years and over compared with the week before (250 fewer deaths).
sourcename: Deaths registered weekly in England and Wales, provisional

title: Caring, leisure and other service occupations saw high COVID-19 death rates
subtitle: Age-standardised mortality rates of death involving the coronavirus (COVID-19) in England and Wales, by major occupational group, deaths registered between 9 March and 28 December 2020
commentary: Between 9 March and 28 December 2020, there were 7,961 deaths involving COVID-19 in the working age population (those aged 20 to 64 years). Almost two-thirds of these deaths (64.4%) were among men, compared with 35.6% among women. Men working in caring, leisure and other services, and elementary occupations had the highest rates of deaths with COVID-19. For women, occupations with the highest rates were process, plant and machine operatives, and caring, leisure and other services.
sourcename: Coronavirus related deaths by occupation

title: Most minority ethnicities have higher COVID-19 mortality rates
subtitle: Rate of death involving coronavirus (COVID-19) by ethnic group and sex relative to the white population, England, 2 March to 28 July 2020
commentary: Death rates for most ethnic minorities are higher compared with White ethnic groups. After accounting for where people live and social and economic factors (including people’s jobs, education and housing conditions), the gap lessens but is still significant.
sourcename: Updating ethnic contrasts in deaths involving the coronavirus (COVID-19), England and Wales

title: Dementia and Alzheimer's disease was the most common pre-existing condition among COVID-19 deaths in England and Wales in 2020
subtitle: The 20 most common pre-existing conditions mentioned in COVID-19 deaths in England and Wales registered in 2020.
commentary: Of deaths in England and Wales where COVID-19 was the underlying cause, the most common pre-existing condition recorded on the death certificate was dementia and Alzheimer's disease. This was identified in around a quarter of COVID-19 deaths. For comparison, dementia and Alzheimer's disease was mentioned in around a fifth of all-cause deaths in England and Wales between 2017 and 2019, a slightly lower proportion. Pre-existing health conditions are recorded on the death certificate if the certifying doctor or coroner believed they made some contribution to the death. Therefore, the death certificate does not include all health conditions the deceased might have suffered from if they were not considered relevant.
sourcename: Monthly mortality analysis, England and Wales

title: Obesity, diabetes and hypertensive diseases are over three times more likely to be pre-existing conditions in COVID-19 deaths than in all-cause deaths
subtitle: Pre-existing conditions with the highest proportional increased rates in COVID-19 deaths in 2020, relative to the mean rate in all-cause deaths in England and Wales between 2017 and 2019 (from the 20 most common pre-existing conditions)
commentary: For deaths occurring in people aged under 65 years, obesity, diabetes and hypertensive diseases were mentioned in three times more COVID-19 deaths than all-cause deaths. Conditions that are mentioned with a higher frequency in deaths due to COVID-19 than in all-cause deaths may indicate increased risk of dying from COVID-19 among people with those conditions.
sourcename: Monthly mortality analysis, England and Wales

title: COVID-19 was the leading cause of death in January 2021 in England and Wales
subtitle: Age-standardised mortality rate for selected leading causes of death, per 100,000 people, England and Wales, deaths registered in January 2021
commentary: In January 2021, the coronavirus (COVID-19) was the leading cause of death in England and Wales for the third consecutive month. In England, there was an age-standardised mortality rate (ASMR) of 545.9 deaths per 100,000 people (25,716 deaths), and in Wales a rate of 539.1 deaths per 100,000 (1,561 deaths). Prior to November 2020, COVID-19 had not been the leading cause of death since May 2020. In January 2021, the rate of deaths due to COVID-19 was significantly higher than the next leading cause of death in both England and Wales.
sourcename: Monthly mortality analysis, England and Wales

title: Hospital admissions of confirmed COVID-19 patients continued to decrease
subtitle: Overall COVID-19 positive hospital admission rates per 100,000, England, weeks ending 9 August 2020 to 28 February 2021
commentary: In the week ending 28 February 2021, the confirmed COVID-19 hospital admission rate in England fell to 8.4 per 100,000 people. The rate is now four times lower than in mid-January.
sourcename: National flu and COVID-19 surveillance reports

title: Hospital admissions and deaths involving COVID-19 continued to decrease in all regions in England
subtitle: Change in hospital admission rates and numbers of deaths involving COVID-19 from previous week, England, weeks ending 28 and 26 February 2021
commentary: In the week ending 28 February 2021, confirmed COVID-19 hospital admission rates decreased in all English regions, with the largest falls recorded in the North West and West Midlands. The West Midlands continued to have the highest hospital admission rate of all regions, at 13.5 per 100,000 people. The number of registered deaths involving COVID-19 fell in all English regions in the week ending 26 February. The largest decreases were seen in the East of England, North West and South East.
sourcename: null

title: The majority of COVID-19 infections are in young people, but hospital admissions and deaths are more common in older age groups
subtitle: Estimated percentage of the population testing positive for COVID-19 in the week ending 27 February 2021, hospital admission rates in the week ending 28 February 2021, and deaths registered in the week ending 26 February 2021, by age, England
commentary: Adults aged 25 to 34 years were most likely to test positive for COVID-19 in the week ending 27 February 2021. Hospital admission rates decreased across all age groups in the week ending 28 February. The largest fall was seen in those aged 85 years and over, although rates in this group remain the highest. While positivity rates were lowest in adults aged 70 years and over, hospital admissions rates and number of deaths involving COVID-19 were the highest in the oldest age groups.
sourcename: null

title: The majority of adults aged 70 years and over reported they have received the vaccine, were awaiting or would be likely to accept it
subtitle: Great Britain, 24 to 28 February 2021
commentary: This week, 94% of adults reported they had now received, are awaiting, or would be likely (very or fairly likely) to have the vaccine if offered.  This proportion increased with age with 99% of adults aged 70 years and over reporting this, compared with 89% of those aged 16 to 29 years.
sourcename: Coronavirus and the social impacts on Great Britain

title: Over 4 in 10 Black or Black British adults reported vaccine hesitancy
subtitle: Great Britain, 13 January to 7 February 2021
commentary: Vaccine hesitancy refers to those who have declined a COVID-19 vaccine offer, report being unlikely to accept a vaccine or report being undecided. Among adults with ethnic minority backgrounds, Black or Black British adults were most likely to report vaccine hesitancy, with 44% of Black or Black British adults reporting hesitancy compared with 8% of White adults.
sourcename: Coronavirus and vaccine hesitancy, Great Britain

title: More young women reported vaccination hesitancy compared with men in the same age group
subtitle: Great Britain, 13 January to 7 February 2021
commentary: Although similar proportions of men and women reported that they would be hesitant towards having a COVID-19 vaccine overall, a slightly higher proportion of younger women (aged 16 to 29 years) reported vaccine hesitancy (19%) compared with men in the same age group (15%). The gap between men and women narrowed for older ager groups.
sourcename: Coronavirus and vaccine hesitancy, Great Britain

title: Adults who were not clinically extremely vulnerable were more likely to report vaccine hesitancy than those who were clinically extremely vulnerable
subtitle: Great Britain, 13 January to 7 February 2021
commentary: Adults who were not clinically extremely vulnerable (CEV) were more likely to report vaccine hesitancy (9%) than those who were clinically extremely vulnerable (4%). Adults without an underlying health condition were more likely to report vaccine hesitancy (10%) than those with an underlying health condition (6%). Disabled and non-disabled adults reported more similar levels of vaccine hesitancy (8% and 9% respectively).
sourcename: Coronavirus and vaccine hesitancy, Great Britain

title: Adults living in the most deprived areas of England were twice as likely to report vaccine hesitancy as adults in the least deprived areas
subtitle: Vaccine hesitancy based on Index of Multiple Deprivation (IMD), England, 13 January to 7 February 2021
commentary: Adults living in the most deprived areas of England were more likely to report vaccine hesitancy (16%) than adults living in the least deprived areas (7%).
sourcename: Coronavirus and vaccine hesitancy, Great Britain

title: The percentage of over 80s who perceived COVID-19 to be a major or significant risk decreased with the number of doses of the vaccine hypothetically received
subtitle: Percentage of all over 80s, by how much they perceived the coronavirus (COVID-19) to be a risk to them personally, after hypothetically receiving each dose of vaccine, England, 15 to 20 February 2021
commentary:
Almost all (99.8%) of adults aged over 80 years reported that they had been offered the COVID-19 vaccination, of which 99% had received at least one dose (15 to 20 February 2021). 
Almost half (49%) of adults aged over 80 years perceived COVID-19 to be a major or significant risk to them personally, before receiving the vaccine. This decreased to 19% when thinking about risk after hypothetically receiving one dose of the vaccine, and further decreased to 5% after hypothetically receiving both doses.
Similarly, the proportion of over 80s who perceived COVID-19 to be a minor or no risk at all, increased with each dose of the vaccine hypothetically received.
sourcename: Coronavirus and vaccine attitudes and behaviours in England: over 80s population

title: The percentage of people with COVID-19 antibodies was highest in England and lowest in Scotland
subtitle: Estimated percentage of people testing positive for antibodies to SARS-CoV-2 from a blood sample, by 28-day periods, 8 May 2020 to 11 February 2021, UK nations
commentary: The percentage of people testing positive for COVID-19 antibodies increased across all four UK nations. In the 28 days up to 11 February 2021, an estimated 1 in 4 people in England, 1 in 6 people in Wales, 1 in 6 people in Northern Ireland and 1 in 8 people in Scotland would have tested positive for antibodies to COVID-19. The presence of antibodies suggests a person has previously had COVID-19, or has been vaccinated.
sourcename: Coronavirus (COVID-19) Infection Survey: antibody data for the UK

title: Antibody positivity was above the national average in London, the North West, the West Midlands, Yorkshire and The Humber and the North East
subtitle: Estimated percentage of people testing positive for antibodies to SARS-CoV-2 from a blood sample, by region, 15 January to 11 February 2021, England
commentary: Antibody positivity increased in all English regions in the 28 days to 1 February 2021, compared with the previous 28-day period to 14 January 2021. There is substantial variation in the percentage testing positive for COVID-19 antibodies across English regions. London had the highest antibody positivity rate at 29.1%, while the lowest antibody positivity rate was in the South West, at 16.3%.
sourcename: Coronavirus (COVID-19) Infection Survey: antibody data for the UK

title: Over 50% of adults aged 80 years and over in England had antibodies against COVID-19
subtitle: Estimated percentage of people testing positive for antibodies to SARS-CoV-2 from a blood sample, by age, 15 January to 11 February 2021, UK nations
commentary: In England, adults aged 80 years and over had the highest antibody postivity rate at 56.4%. However, the true figure for this age group may be different because adults in care homes, who were prioritised for vaccination, are not included in this survey. The second highest antibody positivity rate was seen in those aged 16 to 24 years at 30.1%. The lowest antibody positivity rate was seen in those aged 70 to 74 years at 16.6%. Adults aged 80 years and over in Wales and Scotland had antibody positivity rates of 18.5% and 20.7% respectively. In Northern Ireland, 17.6% of those aged 70 years and over tested positive for antibodies.
sourcename: Coronavirus (COVID-19) Infection Survey: antibody data for the UK

title: Antibody positivity has increased in older ages between 3 January and 11 February 2021
subtitle: Modelled estimated percentage of people testing positive for antibodies to SARS-CoV-2 from a blood sample, by single year of age, from 3 January to 11 February 2021, UK
commentary: In England, antibody positivity more than quadrupled in the oldest ages between 3 January and 11 February. We can examine the changes in antibody positivity over shorter periods by using modelled daily estimates, presented in this graphic. The method used to generate the data differs to the 28-day weighted estimates of antibody positivity so are not comparable.
sourcename: Coronavirus (COVID-19) Infection Survey: antibody data for the UK

title: The Coronavirus (COVID-19) Infection Survey and REACT-2 show that antibody positivity increased
subtitle: Estimated percentage of the community population testing positive for antibodies to SARS-CoV-2, 8 May 2020 to 11 February 2021, England
commentary: The proportion of people testing positive for antibodies to COVID-19 in England has increased, according to both the Coronavirus (COVID-19) Infection Survey (CIS, 15 January to 11 February 2021) and the Real-time Assessment of Community Transmission (REACT) study (26 January to 8 February 2021). REACT and CIS show similar trends over time,  with REACT estimates being slightly lower. This might be because REACT uses self-administered tests and in CIS a blood sample is taken by a health professional. In the most recent period the REACT estimate is notably lower than CIS, which may reflect a low proportion of vaccinated people among REACT participants (11%).
sourcename: Real-time Assessment of Community Transmission (REACT) study

title: Women consistently spent more time on unpaid childcare and household work than men
subtitle: Working from home, unpaid childcare and household work, across Great Britain and the UK, in 2014 to 2015, March to April 2020, and September to October 2020
commentary: While both men and women spent more time working from home during the pandemic, women spent more time on unpaid household work and unpaid childcare than men. In September and October 2020, women spent 64% more time on unpaid household work. In March and April 2020, women spent 55% more time on unpaid childcare. However, this difference is smaller than in September and October 2020, when women spent 99% more time on unpaid childcare than men. In January and February 2021, a greater proportion of women (67%) than men (52%) homeschooled a school-aged child.
sourcename: Coronavirus (COVID-19) and the different effects on men and women in the UK, March 2020 to February 2021

title: Women reported higher anxiety, depression and loneliness than men
subtitle: Anxiety, lonely at some point, and moderate to severe depressive symptoms, Great Britain, March 2020 to January 2021.
commentary: Women reported significantly higher anxiety than men at almost every point between March 2020 and February 2021, continuing the pre-pandemic trend. Loneliness was found to be the strongest driver of anxiety in the early stages of the pandemic, with women being 1.3 times more likely to report loneliness than men. The difference between men's and women's level of loneliness and depressive symptoms was largest from June 2020 onwards.
sourcename: Coronavirus (COVID-19) and the different effects on men and women in the UK, March 2020 to February 2021

title: Compliance with preventative measures remains high
subtitle: Great Britain, 24 to 28 February 2021
commentary: There are several measures in place to help curb the spread of COVID-19, such as handwashing, use of face coverings, avoiding physical contact and self-isolating. Compliance with most measures remained high this week (24 to 28 February 2021), with 88% of adults reporting always or often handwashing after returning home, 95% using a face covering and 92% avoiding physical contact when outside their home. This week, 86% of adults reported always or often maintaining social distance when meeting up with other people outside their support bubble.
sourcename: Coronavirus and the social impacts on Great Britain

title: All four personal well-being scores improved slightly in the latest week
subtitle: Great Britain, March 2020 to February 2021
commentary:
The level of life satisfaction (6.6) and feeling that things done in life are worthwhile (7.1) improved slightly this week (24 to 28 February 2021). There has been a gradual improvement in the level of happiness (6.7 this week), since a lowest level recorded on this survey in January (6.4 in the periods 13 to 31 January). The level of anxiety (4.0 this week) has gradually improved since a recent high in early January (4.6 in the period 7 to 10 January).
These scores are answered on a scale of 0 to to 10, where 0 is "not at all" and 10 is "completely".
sourcename: Coronavirus and the social impacts on Great Britain

title: The proportion of adults who felt that it will take less than six months for life to return to normal continued to increase
subtitle: Great Britain, March 2020 to February 2021
commentary: The proportion of adults who felt that it will take less than six months for life to return to normal increased to 32% in the latest week (24 to 28 February 2021) from 22% the week before. The proportion of adults who felt that it will take more than a year for life to return to normal decreased to 20% from 27% in the previous week.
sourcename: Coronavirus and the social impacts on Great Britain

title: Half of parents who were homeschooling agreed that it was negatively affecting their well-being
subtitle: Percentage of homeschooling parents who agreed with the statement on homeschooling, Great Britain, 3 April to 10 May 2020 and 13 January to 7 February 2021
commentary: Between 13 January and 7 February 2021, 9 in 10 (90%) of parents with a school-age child said that a child in their household had been homeschooled in the past seven days because of the coronavirus pandemic. Half (50%) of homeschooling parents said that homeschooling had a negative effect on their well-being in January 2021, an increase from 28% in April 2020. Almost two-thirds (63%) said that homeschooling had a negative effect on their children's well-being, an increase from 43% in April 2020.
sourcename: Coronavirus and the social impact on Great Britain: Exploring behaviours during the different lockdown periods

title: Some ethnic groups are more likely to work in jobs with higher COVID-19 death rates
subtitle: Proportion of ethnic group within occupations and COVID-19 death rate, England and Wales, deaths involving COVID-19 registered between 9 March and 25 May 2020
commentary: Black and Asian men are more likely to work in occupations that have had a higher risk of death involving COVID-19, such as transport, security and cleaning. For working women, there were higher rates of death involving COVID-19 in four professions including nursing, and people working as care workers or home carers. Of women working as care workers and home carers, a relatively high proportion were from Black ethnic backgrounds (13.2%). There were also higher proportions of women in nursing from Indian, Black and Other ethnic backgrounds.
sourcename: Coronavirus (COVID-19) related deaths by occupation, England and Wales

title: Multi-generational households with someone aged 70 years and older are more common for people of Bangladeshi or Pakistani ethnicity
subtitle: Proportion of households with at least one person aged 70 years or over by ethnic group of that person, by mix of ages in the household, UK, 2018
commentary: During the first national lockdown, people in the more vulnerable, older age groups were asked to shield and minimise contact with other people to reduce their risk of infection. Older people living in larger households may have found it more difficult to shield practically. Multi-generational households are much more common among ethnic minority groups, particularly those in the Pakistani, Bangladeshi or Indian ethnic groups.
sourcename: Coronavirus (COVID-19) roundup

title: People from minority ethnic groups are less likely to have access to a private garden
subtitle: Percentage of people with access to a private garden, by ethnic group, England, 2014 to 2019
commentary: During lockdown, many people found solace in a garden or outdoor space. In England, those in the Black ethnic group are nearly four times as likely as people in the White ethnic group to have no outdoor space at home (37% compared with 10%) – that is no private or shared garden, a patio or a balcony. After accounting for urban and rural living, age, social class, and whether they had children, the statistics remained significantly different.
sourcename: One in eight British households has no garden

title: Most ethnicity groups reported worse mental health during the pandemic
subtitle: Fully adjusted average change in GHQ-12 scores of those aged 16 years and over between 2019 and April 2020 by ethnic group, UK, 2019 and April 2020
commentary: Over a third (36%) of those from the Indian ethnic group reported increased or persistent loss of sleep over worry, compared with less than a quarter (23%) of White British respondents and 18% of those in the Other White ethnic groups. Around a third of those from the Black, African, Caribbean or Black British ethnic group (35%) also reported this.
sourcename: Coronavirus and the social impacts on different ethnic groups in the UK: 2020

title: Percentage of school staff testing positive for antibodies to COVID-19, England
subtitle: Percentage of staff testing positive for antibodies to COVID-19 in primary and secondary schools, measured between 3 to 19 November 2020 (round 1) and 2 to 10 December 2020 (round 2), England
commentary: In the first round of testing (3 to 19 November 2020), 12.6% of staff working in primary schools and 12.3% in secondary schools tested positive for antibodies based on blood tests. In the second round of testing (2 to 10 December 2020), these increased to 14.6% for primary school staff and 15.7%  for secondary school staff. Caution is needed when interpreting these results because of the small sample sizes.
sourcename: COVID-19 Schools Infection Survey Round 2, England: December 2020

title: Percentage of pupils testing positive for antibodies to COVID-19, England
subtitle: Percentage of pupils testing positive for antibodies to COVID-19 in primary and secondary schools, measured between 3 to 19 November 2020 (round 1) and 2 to 10 December 2020 (round 2), England
commentary: In the first round of testing (3 to 19 November 2020), 7.7% of primary school pupils and 11% of secondary school pupils tested positive for antibodies to COVID-19 based on oral fluids. Currently, pupil antibody data are only available for Round 1. Caution is needed when interpreting these results because of the small sample sizes and low response rates in pupils.
sourcename: COVID-19 Schools Infection Survey Round 2, England: December 2020

title: Percentage of staff and pupils testing positive for current COVID-19 infection, England
subtitle: Percentage of staff and pupils testing positive for current COVID-19 infection in primary and secondary schools, measured between 3 to 19 November 2020 (round 1) and 2 to 10 December 2020 (round 2), England
commentary: In both the first (3 to 19 November 2020) and second (2 to 10 December 2020) rounds of testing, current infection estimates for COVID-19 were higher in secondary than in primary school pupils and staff. However, caution is needed when interpreting the test results because of the small sample sizes, and low response rates in pupils. In the second round of testing (2 to 10 December 2020), 1.64% of secondary school staff tested positive for current infection compared with 0.99% of primary school staff. In the same period, the proportion of pupils testing positive for current infection was 1.22% in secondary schools and 0.94% in primary schools.
sourcename: COVID-19 Schools Infection Survey Round 2, England: December 2021

title: Most students’ mental health has worsened as a result of the pandemic
subtitle: Responses from students to "how has the coronavirus impacted your mental health?", UK, 2020
commentary: According to a survey of university students in 2020, 57% reported their mental health was either a little worse (43%) or much worse (15%) because of the coronavirus pandemic. Over a quarter (28%) said their mental health was the same, and 15% said their mental health was either a little better or much better since the pandemic. Findings from a variety of studies looking at student behaviours and wellbeing, including the ONS’s Student COVID-19 Insights Survey, have been presented in Coronavirus and the impact on students in higher education in England: September to December 2020.
sourcename: Coronavirus and the impact on students in higher education in England: September to December 2020

title: Fewer students report high well-being compared with others aged 20 to 24 years
subtitle: Personal well-being measures scoring “very high” for full-time undergraduate students and for young people aged 20 to 24 years, UK, 2016 to 2020
commentary: Prior to the coronavirus pandemic, student well-being had been decreasing over the last four years, according to data from the Student Academic Experience Survey. On four main measures of personal well-being (life satisfaction, feelings that things done in life are worthwhile, happiness, low anxiety), undergraduate students report substantially lower levels of well-being compared with the general population aged 20 to 24 years. However, different collection methods used in the surveys completed by students and the wider population could contribute to this difference.
sourcename: Coronavirus and the impact on students in higher education in England: September to December 2020

title: COVID-19 cases among students at Exeter University rose sharply following the start of term
subtitle: All cases among students by day, and NHS testing cases by day for those aged over 21 years in Exeter, 2 September 2020 to 16 November 2020
commentary: Data from Exeter University showed a high number of COVID-19 cases among students in the city following the start of term in September 2020. In contrast, cases among the wider population of Exeter rose steadily throughout the autumn. It is not possible to determine from this whether the arrival of students in Exeter had an impact on the rising levels of COVID-19 in the wider community, as infections were also increasing across the country during the autumn.
sourcename: How has coronavirus (COVID-19) spread among students in England?

title: In recent weeks, the proportion of adults staying at home or only leaving for essential needs remains higher than during the winter 2020 restrictions
subtitle: Percentage of adults that reported staying at home or only leaving for work, exercise, essential shopping or medical needs and daily road traffic index, Great Britain, May 2020 to February 2021
commentary: Despite recent decreases, the proportion of adults reporting staying at home or only leaving for work, exercise, essential shopping or medical needs (56%, 3 to 7 February 2021) remains higher than during the winter 2020 restrictions (prior to the early 2021 lockdown). The volume of car traffic was reduced to a similar level in the early 2021 lockdown (51% of the level observed in the first week of February 2020) as seen in the spring 2020 lockdown (51% between 14 and 17 May 2020).
sourcename: Coronavirus and the social impact on Great Britain: Exploring behaviours during the different lockdown periods

title: The likelihood of testing positive for the coronavirus (COVID-19) varies across occupations
subtitle:
Likelihood of testing positive for COVID-19 by occupation, based on model adjusting for demographics, ease of social distancing at work, use of face coverings at work and working at home or elsewhere, 1 September 2020 to 7 January 2021, England.
Brackets indicate occupations that are unlikely to have evidence of difference in the probability of people testing positive compared to many other occupations in the same bracket.
commentary:
Across 25 occupations, the likelihood of testing positive for COVID-19 between 1 September 2020 and 7 January 2021 ranged from 2.1% to 4.8%.
The occupations towards the higher end of the range were: caring personal service occupations, protective service occupations, teaching and other education professionals, secretarial and related occupations, and other managers and proprietors. These occupations had statistically significantly higher likelihood of testing positive than some at the lower end, but not those in the middle of the range. At the lower end were: skilled agricultural and related trades; science, research, engineering and technology professionals; business, media and public service professionals; and textiles, printing and other skilled trades.
sourcename: Coronavirus (COVID-19) Infection Survey: characteristics of people testing positive for COVID-19 in England

title: COVID-19 mortality risk for most disabled groups is higher than non-disabled groups, although the risk is substantially reduced after adjusting for other characteristics
subtitle: Hazard ratios for death involving COVID-19 for disabled men and women relative to non-disabled people of the same sex, adjusting for age, residence type, geography, socio-economic and demographic factors, and comorbidities, England: 24 January to 20 November 2020
commentary: After adjusting for a range of factors, compared with non-disabled people, an increased risk of death involving COVID-19 remained for more-disabled and less-disabled women (1.4 and 1.2 times respectively) and more-disabled men (1.1 times) but not for less-disabled men. Disability status was defined according to the 2011 Census, with more-disabled and less-disabled referring to people who reported their daily activities as "limited a lot" or "limited a little", respectively.
sourcename: Updated estimates of coronavirus (COVID-19) related deaths by disability status, England: 24 January to 20 November 2020

title: COVID-19 mortality risk for people with a learning disability is higher than for people with no learning disability, although risk is substantially reduced after adjusting for other characteristics
subtitle: Hazard ratios for death involving COVID-19 for men and women with a learning disability relative to people with no learning disability of the same sex, adjusting for age, residence type, geography, socio-economic and demographic factors, and comorbidities, England: 24 January to 20 November 2020
commentary: After adjusting for a range of factors, people with a diagnosed learning disability remained at greater risk (1.7 times) of COVID-19 mortality than with those with no learning disability.
sourcename: Updated estimates of coronavirus (COVID-19) related deaths by disability status, England: 24 January to 20 November 2020
